title: Distributed tracing in practice
subtitle: A trace shows where one request spent its time across many services. Learn to pass the trace ID along and read the waterfall.

q.v: and calls the next service. What should it send?

options.v: The same trace ID, a new parent ID (its own span ID), and the flags.
A new trace ID, because each service starts its own trace.

why.v: The trace ID stays the same for the whole request. The parent ID must change to the ID of the current operation, so the next span knows its parent.

q.v: A trace shows 40 ms between the start of a client span and the start of the matching server span. Nothing else is recorded there. What is the most likely cause?

options.v: Waiting that has no span, such as a queue, a proxy or a full thread pool.

why.v: A gap means time passed that nobody recorded. Queue wait and code without instrumentation are the usual causes. A slow database call would show up as its own span. Clock skew can also shift a server span, so check that if the gap looks odd.

q.v: You want to keep every trace that has an error, while storing only 5% of normal traces. Which approach can do this?

options.v: Turning off sampling for errors in the sampled flag.

why.v: Head-based sampling decides at the start, before anyone knows the request will fail. Only a decision made after the trace ends can look for errors.

q.v: In a waterfall, a request takes 500 ms. A cache call takes 20 ms and runs in parallel with a 300 ms pricing call. Nothing else runs at the same time. Which change makes the request faster?

options.v: Making the cache call 10 ms faster.
Making the pricing call 100 ms faster.

why.v: The pricing call is on the critical path. The cache call already finishes while pricing is still running, so making it faster changes nothing.
